review_scope: Complete 107-line adoption guidance, 24-line utility model concept, 42-line base/LTS concept and six-line utility list read. All metadata, categories, preview boundaries, enablement timeline and exceptions retained. No live service assertions, linked terms clearance, independent omission audit or policy acceptance.

claims.statement: This governance guidance declares the Copilot cloud feature; it does not independently establish target plan, entitlement or administrator permissions.
Enterprise administrators are advised to track capabilities, adoption timing and risk across organizations; this guidance is not a configured control.
Docs, the Copilot blog and changelog are recommended release-monitoring sources; linked announcements are not verified by this pinned-artifact review.

The assistive category requires human review and user approval before changes, with inline suggestions, chat and pull-request assistance as examples; category wording does not prove every product operation is gated.
Agentic capabilities can research, plan and change autonomously under stated built-in protections; actual protection behavior needs independent testing.
Customization support and configuration vary by feature and surface; some access is controllable at organization or enterprise level, not necessarily all customization.
External agents, models and tools are categorized with agentic capabilities; provider documentation and policy enablement are separate review requirements.
New features have distinct enablement requirements; guidance recommends capability review, enterprise/organization policy inspection and a subset-user pilot before broad rollout.
Model characteristics differ, and user access depends on feature, enterprise plan and policy; a model catalog entry alone is not permission or availability.
Supported models, comparison and changelog are separate model evidence sources; this review does not adopt their linked contents.
Utility models power background features and cannot be disabled by enterprise model choices; compliance monitoring must not assume an ordinary model deny covers them.
The base-model category is a default when no other models are enabled and describes automatic enablement within 60 days of designation.
The LTS category describes one year of support from designation, not immutable outputs, pricing or perpetual availability.
Utility/base/LTS and default-availability dependencies refine the category overview; prior default-policy review is not duplicated.
Release stages have differing stability and support expectations; the broad GA all-customers description remains bounded by the article's feature/plan/policy access constraints.
Private previews are invitation-limited and may change significantly.
Public previews require eligible customers to opt in and can have limitations or change.
The source describes GA as fully supported and production-recommended, not a guarantee of target compliance, safety or entitlement.
The source says many previews are DPA-covered and links a specific coverage list; this is not universal preview coverage or legal clearance for a particular use.
The preview opt-in policy described here specifically concerns the GitHub website; it must not be generalized to all clients or external agents.
Per-feature responsible-use articles are transparency references for purpose/capability/limitations; linking them does not complete their review.
Utility-model concept scope declares the Copilot cloud feature; actual account/client deployment is not observed.
Utility models are automatically enabled across every Copilot plan and power background tasks such as commit messages or session titles.
Utility-model scope spans IDEs, GitHub, CLI and the Copilot app rather than only the website.
Utility models are hidden from the model picker and cannot be selected directly; absence from that UI is not absence of model processing.
Organization and enterprise administrators cannot disable utility models except by disabling Copilot completely; per-model policy is not a complete deny boundary.
Utility usage is described as consuming neither premium request units nor usage-based billing tokens and not appearing as a billed line item; billing visibility is not processing absence.
Utility models have per-user rate limits and operate irrespective of ordinary model policies/billing controls; rate limits are not enumerated in this artifact.
The utility list is separately reusable and typically favors lightweight models; selection heuristics are not a fixed contractual model set.
The base/LTS concepts declare Copilot cloud scope, not GHES availability.

The pin states a March 18, 2026 base-model designation through the GPT-5.3-Codex variable and restricts base-model applicability to Business/Enterprise; this historical source statement is not current runtime proof.
Base models serve when no other models are enabled and become automatically enabled for Business/Enterprise accounts within 60 days of designation.
The base transition begins with an announcement on day zero.
The documented upgrade window gives customers day zero through day sixty to install IDE extensions supporting the new base model.
The timeline specifies day-sixty automatic enablement across organizations and enterprises; this can override assumptions of permanently unconfigured/disabled model availability.
The pin separately states a March 18, 2026 LTS designation through the same model variable and applies LTS only to Business/Enterprise.
LTS support lasts one year from designation and promises model availability during that period; it does not establish immutable behavior or an independently verified service commitment.
Supported-model and billing/pricing links remain separate evidence, not silently ingested current capabilities or prices.

The pinned utility list names four variable identities: copilot_gpt_4o_mini, copilot_gpt_4o, copilot_gpt_41 and copilot_gpt_54_nano. Variable names and pinned list membership are not current enabled-target evidence.
